items.title: Vector and transmission cycle
items.contentHtml:
Vector and transmission cycle

  • Ixodes scapularis (black-legged tick) is the primary vector in the northeastern United States; Ixodes ricinus in Europe.
  • Transmission occurs by nymphs, not by adults; the feeding period required to inoculate Babesia is usually >24-36 hours.
  • The main reservoir is small rodents, especially the white-footed mouse (Peromyscus leucopus).
  • Babesiosis is not transmitted from person to person by direct contact; The non-vector route includes blood transfusion and congenital transmission.

items.foco: Blood culture not useful for diagnosis
items.title: Diagnosis: useless blood culture
items.contentHtml:
Diagnosis: useless blood culture

  • Conventional blood culture is not useful because Babesia is an intraerythrocytic parasite that does not grow in standard bacterial media.
  • Definitive diagnosis is based on direct visualization of the parasite in peripheral blood smears stained with Giemsa or Wright.
  • Parasitemia may be low at the beginning; repeat the smear every 12-24 hours if suspicion is high.
  • inoculation in animals (hamster or gerbil) is an experimental technique, not available in routine clinical practice.

items.title: Smear and thick smear
items.contentHtml:
Smear and thick smear

  • The thick smear concentrates parasites and increases sensitivity, but the thin smear allows identification of the species and morphology.
  • In the thin smear, Babesia trophozoites appear as intraerythrocytic rings similar to Plasmodium falciparum.
  • The tetrad (Maltese cross shape) is pathognomonic but is seen in less than 5% of cases.
  • Parasitemia >4% is associated with severe disease; The count is expressed as a percentage of infected erythrocytes.

items.title: PCR in diagnosis
items.contentHtml:
PCR in diagnosis

  • The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) has high sensitivity and specificity, especially useful in low parasitemias or when the smear is negative.
  • PCR can detect Babesia DNA even after treatment, so it should not be used to monitor cure.
  • It is recommended in cases of high clinical suspicion with a negative smear, and in blood donors for screening in endemic areas.
  • PCR does not differentiate between active and past infection if used qualitatively; Quantitative load can be correlated with severity.

items.title: Morphology: tetrad
items.contentHtml:
Morphology: tetrad

  • The tetrad (also called Maltese cross) consists of four merozoites within an erythrocyte, the product of asexual division.
  • It is highly suggestive of babesiosis, but its absence does not exclude the diagnosis.
  • In the thin extension, the rings can have a vacuole, but unlike Plasmodium there is no malarial pigment (hemozoin).
  • The observation of extracellular forms (broken erythrocytes) is common in babesiosis, rare in malaria.

items.title: Severity risk factors
items.contentHtml:
Severity risk factors

  • Splenectomy is the most important risk factor for severe disease, with high parasitemias and a fulminant course.
  • Other factors: age >50 years, immunosuppression (HIV/AIDS, transplant, biological therapy), underlying cardiovascular or liver disease.
  • In asplenic patients, parasitemia can exceed the 70% and cause multiple organ failure.
  • Coinfection with Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease) can also increase the severity.

items.title: most common species
items.contentHtml:
Most common species

  • Babesia microti is the most common species in humans in the United States, transmitted by Ixodes scapularis.
  • In Europe, Babesia divergens is the main species, associated with cattle and with greater severity in splenectomized cattle.
  • Babesia duncani has been described on the west coast of the United States.
  • The species Babesia venatorum (EU1) has been reported in Europe and Asia.

items.title: First line treatment
items.contentHtml:
First-line treatment

  • The regimen of choice for mild-moderate disease is atovaquone (750 mg every 12 hours) plus azithromycin (500 mg on the first day, then 250 mg/day) orally for 7-10 days.
  • This combination has fewer adverse effects than the alternative with quinine.
  • In patients immunocompromised or with severe disease, treatment can be prolonged up to 6 weeks or more, with monitoring for parasitemia.
  • Atovaquone acts by inhibiting the parasite's mitochondrial electron transport.

items.title: Tratamiento alternativo
items.contentHtml:
Tratamiento alternativo

  • La combinación clindamicina (600 mg cada 8 horas) más quinina (650 mg cada 6-8 horas) es la alternativa clásica, especialmente en enfermedad grave o si hay alergia a atovacuona.
  • Este esquema se asocia con más efectos adversos: cinconismo, hipoglucemia, arritmias (prolongación QT), y tinnitus.
  • En pacientes con parasitemia >10% o complicaciones graves, se recomienda exanguinotransfusión además del tratamiento antiparasitario.
  • La clindamicina se administra intravenosa en casos severos.

items.title: blood transfusion
items.contentHtml:
Transmisión transfusional

  • La babesiosis es la infección transmitida por transfusión más reportada en Estados Unidos, con Babesia microti como principal agente.
  • Los eritrocitos contaminados pueden permanecer viables durante la refrigeración (hasta 35 días) y sobrevivir a la leucorreducción.
  • El riesgo es mayor en donantes asintomáticos con parasitemia baja y persistente.
  • El screening de donantes se realiza en áreas endémicas mediante anticuerpos y PCR; la infección puede ser fatal en receptores inmunocomprometidos o asplénicos.

items.title: Clinical picture: hemolytic anemia
items.contentHtml:
Clinical picture: hemolytic anemia

  • The typical presentation is fever, fatigue, headache, myalgia, and hemolytic anemia with jaundice and splenomegaly.
  • Hemolysis is intravascular and extravascular, with increased lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and indirect bilirubin, decreased haptoglobin, and reticulocytosis.
  • Thrombocytopenia may occur.
  • Thrombocytopenia may occur. and leukopenia, but disseminated intravascular coagulation is rare.
  • In severe cases: acute renal failure, acute respiratory distress syndrome, shock.

items.title: Coinfección con Borrelia burgdorferi
items.contentHtml:
Coinfection with Borrelia burgdorferi

  • Both infections share the Ixodes scapularis vector, so coinfection is possible in up to 10-15% of patients with Lyme disease.
  • Presentation may include persistent fever, arthritis, erythema migrans, and constitutional symptoms that do not respond to doxycycline alone.
  • If coinfection is suspected, should treat both: doxycycline for Borrelia burgdorferi and babesiosis regimen.
  • Coinfection can cause more severe and prolonged disease, with a higher risk of complications.
